screens.title: Orchestrating Containers with Amazon ECS and Fargate
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we shift from building container images to running them reliably at scale. You will learn what makes up Amazon ECS—clusters, task definitions, tasks, and services—and why choosing the right launch type matters. We'll focus on the Fargate launch type so you can run containers without provisioning EC2 instances. That means specifying C P U, memory, and networking while AWS handles the underlying servers. Practically, you'll see how to create a Fargate cluster, author a task definition that points to an image in ECR, and create a service that integrates with an Application Load Balancer. I will also explain how to enable service auto-scaling and the common misconfigurations that prevent tasks from running, such as missing permissions on the ecsTaskExecutionRole or incorrect security group rules. By the end of this lesson you'll understand the deployment flow and the safety checklist you should run before launching a production service. To ground this, we'll use an Nginx example pushed to ECR and deploy it to an ALB-backed, auto-scaled Fargate service so you can verify the DNS and clean up resources afterward. Ready to deploy your first Fargate service and reduce operational overhead?

screens.title: ECS Core Components
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the four core ECS concepts and why each matters. A cluster is a logical collection where tasks and services run. Think of it as a name and grouping that can be backed by EC2 instances or Fargate; the choice affects who manages servers. A task definition is a declarative blueprint describing one or more containers, their images, C P U and memory, port mappings, networking mode, environment variables, and the execution IAM role. It is the unit you version and deploy. A task is an instantiation of that definition — one running set of containers. It lives inside a cluster and consumes the defined resources. A service ties the pieces together by specifying how many copies of the task should be running, performing health checks and restarting tasks when needed. Services also integrate with load balancers so traffic can be routed to healthy tasks. Common confusion comes from language: a task definition is not a running container, and a service is not a task; the service manages tasks created from a task definition. For example, when you update a task definition you must update the service to use the new revision so ECS will launch replacement tasks with the new configuration. Verify your ecsTaskExecutionRole and network settings before launching a service to avoid failures.

keyIdea.text: Cluster groups, task definitions describe containers, tasks run those containers, and services maintain desired task counts and integrate with load balancers.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › ECS Components
Definitions
Clear definitions reduce deployment mistakes. Read these before authoring a task definition or creating a service.
Cluster
Logical grouping of tasks and services. Can be backed by EC2 or Fargate.
Task Definition
Blueprint describing containers, resources, ports, network mode, and execution role.
Task
A running instantiation of a task definition.
Service
Maintains a desired number of tasks and integrates with load balancers.
Practical example
Imagine you register a task definition named my-web-app-task-def. When you create a service using that definition and set desired tasks to 2, ECS will run two task instances of that definition inside your cluster. If a task fails health checks, the service replaces it.
Key Takeaway
Know which artifact is a definition, which is a running instance, and which object manages availability.
Common mistake
Confusing task definition with a running task; updating a task definition alone does not change running tasks until the service is updated.

screens.title: EC2 vs Fargate Launch Types
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between EC2 and Fargate affects cost, control, and operational tasks. EC2 launch type gives you full control over worker nodes: you provision and patch EC2 instances, choose instance families, and can optimize cost with Reserved or Spot Instances for stable, predictable workloads. That control can yield cost savings for long-running services, but it requires you to manage capacity, OS updates, and scaling rules. Fargate abstracts away the nodes. You simply define C P U and memory for your tasks and AWS runs them. This serverless model minimizes operational overhead and charges you only for the C P U and memory your tasks use. It is ideal for variable or unpredictable workloads and for teams that want to focus on application logic. A common misconception is that Fargate is always more expensive; while Fargate can have higher per-unit costs, the operational savings and pay-per-use model often justify it for many workloads. Use EC2 when you need custom AMIs, specialized drivers, or deeper control over the host. Use Fargate for simplicity, faster onboarding, and consistent, serverless container execution. EC2 vs Fargate Launch Types means ec2 offers control and potential cost optimization for predictable workloads; fargate offers serverless simplicity and pay-for-use billing.. In practical terms, when to manage ec2 instances and when to use serverless fargate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Launch Type Comparison
EC2 Launch Type
You manage the instances. Use custom AMIs, tune the OS, and utilize Spot or Reserved Instances for cost control.
  • Full node control and customization.
  • Operational overhead: patching, scaling, and instance lifecycle.
  • Best for predictable, long-running workloads.
When to pick EC2: need host-level access or custom drivers.
Fargate Launch Type
Serverless compute for containers. Specify resources per task and let AWS provision and maintain the infrastructure.
  • No EC2 instance management required.
  • Pay for CPU and memory consumed by tasks.
  • Ideal for variable or unpredictable workloads.
When to pick Fargate: reduce ops, faster deployments, serverless billing.
Misconception
Fargate is always more expensive. Evaluate total cost including operational time and utilization.
Pro tip
Prototype on Fargate for speed, then evaluate EC2 if you need host customizations or long-term cost optimizations.
Check
Confirm your workload's network and dependency requirements before choosing the launch type.

screens.title: Deploying a Web App to Fargate — Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk the deployment process step by step so you can repeat it reliably. Step one is creating a Fargate cluster; this reserves a logical environment name and readies ECS for tasks. Step two is authoring a task definition that specifies networkMode as awsvpc, an execution role, container image, port mapping, C P U, and memory. Step three registers that task definition and optionally uploads a JSON file via the CLI. Step four creates an Application Load Balancer and a target group configured for IP targets and an appropriate health check path. Step five creates the ECS service: choose Fargate, select the task definition, set the desired task count, and attach the target group so the ALB routes traffic to tasks. Finally, enable service auto-scaling with policies such as scale-out when C P U > 70 percent and scale-in when C P U < 50 percent. A common pitfall is forgetting to open port 80 in the ALB and task security groups, which blocks traffic even when tasks are running. Follow this process and verify each step with describe commands or the console status until the ALB returns the expected page.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Deployment Steps
Deployment steps (process)
1. Create Fargate cluster
Name it, then use it when creating services.
2. Register Task Definition
Specify awsvpc, ecsTaskExecutionRole, image URI, CPU, memory, and port mappings.
3. Create ALB & Target Group
Target type: ip, health check path: /. Configure listener on port 80.
4. Create Service
Choose task definition and attach ALB target group. Set desired count.
5. Configure Auto-Scaling
Use CPU or custom metrics, set scale-out and scale-in thresholds.
Example verification checklist
  • Tasks move to RUNNING state.
  • Target group shows healthy targets.
  • ALB DNS returns the application page.
  • CloudWatch logs show container startup messages.
Common mistake
Forgetting to allow traffic between ALB and task security groups will prevent successful HTTP responses even when tasks are healthy.

screens.title: Task Definition JSON Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Now we will examine a minimal task definition and explain the fields you must set for Fargate. The family names the task definition revision. Network mode must be awsvpc for Fargate to provide an elastic network interface per task. C P U and memory are specified as strings representing task-level resources. executionRoleArn should point to ecsTaskExecutionRole so the ECS agent can pull images from ECR and publish logs to CloudWatch. Under containerDefinitions you list each container with its image, port mappings, log configuration, and resource settings. Port mappings are needed for ALB routing. A frequent error is omitting the awslogs configuration so container logs do not arrive in CloudWatch, which makes troubleshooting harder. Another common issue is specifying too little C P U or memory; monitor CloudWatch to determine if tasks are throttled or crash. Use this JSON as a starting point, replace the ECR image URI with your repo, and register it using the AWS CLI register-task-definition command. This concrete example helps you avoid the most common omissions when authoring task definitions. In practical terms, a minimal fargate task definition and important fields. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Task Definition
Minimal Fargate task definition (JSON)
{
  "family": "my-web-app-task-def",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "cpu": "256",
  "memory": "512",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole",
  "containerDefinitions": [
    {
      "name": "my-web-app-container",
      "image": "YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-web-app:latest",
      "portMappings": [ { "containerPort": 80, "protocol": "tcp" } ],
      "essential": true,
      "logConfiguration": {
        "logDriver": "awslogs",
        "options": {
          "awslogs-group": "/ecs/my-web-app",
          "awslogs-region": "us-east-1",
          "awslogs-stream-prefix": "ecs"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"]
}
Field explanations
  • requiresCompatibilities: set to FARGATE for serverless tasks.
  • networkMode: awsvpc assigns ENIs to tasks and is required for Fargate.
  • executionRoleArn: grants ECS permissions to pull images and write logs.
  • logConfiguration: enables CloudWatch logs for troubleshooting.
Tip: replace placeholder ARN and image URI with your account values before registering.
Key Takeaway
Author task definitions carefully: missing execution role or logs will break startup or make debugging difficult.

screens.title: Service, ALB, and Target Group Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding how the Application Load Balancer connects to Fargate tasks is essential for validating deployments. In this architecture, an ALB listener receives HTTP traffic on port 80 and forwards it to a target group configured with target type ip. Each Fargate task receives an elastic network interface and an IP in your selected subnets, so the target group registers the task IPs as targets. Configure a health check path, for example root slash, that returns 200 OK so the ALB knows which targets are healthy. If a target fails health checks, the ALB removes it from routing and the ECS service will try to replace it to maintain the desired count. Security groups must permit inbound traffic from the ALB to the task on the container port, and the ALB's security group must permit inbound 80 from the internet or your client. Misconfigurations often involve security groups or health checks pointing to the wrong path. Always verify the ALB target group shows healthy targets before concluding the deployment is successful. Service, ALB, and Target Group Architecture means alb listener → target group (ip targets) → fargate task enis; health checks remove unhealthy targets and services replace failed tasks.. In practical terms, how alb routes traffic to fargate tasks and health checks keep services healthy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › ALB & Target Groups
Architecture summary
ALB routes incoming requests to the target group. For Fargate use target type ip so task ENIs are reachable by the ALB.
ALB Listener (HTTP 80)
Target Group (target-type: ip)
Fargate Tasks with ENIs and container port 80
Configuration checklist
  • Target group health check path set to application health endpoint.
  • Task security group allows inbound traffic from ALB security group on container port.
  • ALB registered in at least two subnets for high availability.
Common issue: health checks mispointed to a path that returns non-200 responses.
Key Takeaway
Verify security groups, health check path, and that target type is ip when using Fargate.

screens.title: Hands-on CLI Steps
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough gives command examples you can run in the terminal to automate the deployment. First create the cluster with aws ecs create-cluster. Next create an ALB, target group, and listener using the elbv2 create-load-balancer, create-target-group, and create-listener commands. Use target-type ip and configure health check settings. Then author your task definition JSON with networkMode awsvpc and register it using aws ecs register-task-definition. Finally, assemble the service JSON referencing the cluster name, task definition, desired count, networkConfiguration with subnets and security group IDs, and a loadBalancers block with the target group ARN. Create the service with aws ecs create-service and monitor status using aws ecs describe-services and aws ecs describe-tasks. If tasks stay in PENDING or stop immediately, inspect CloudWatch logs and the ecs agent error messages. This CLI sequence mirrors the console flow and helps you automate repeatable deployments for CI/CD pipelines. Hands-on CLI Steps means use ecs and elbv2 cli commands to script cluster creation, alb and target group setup, task registration, and service creation.. In practical terms, commands to create cluster, alb, target group, register task, and create service. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Essential commands

screens.title: Service Auto-Scaling and Health Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Service auto-scaling ensures your application can handle changes in load without manual intervention. Start by enabling service auto-scaling for your ECS service and create a scalable target. Common policies use C P U or memory utilization as the metric. For example, set a scale-out policy that adds tasks when C P U crosses 70 percent and a scale-in policy that removes tasks below 50 percent. Choose cooldown periods and minimum and maximum task counts to prevent rapid flapping. Health checks are equally important: configure the ALB target group's health check path to your application's readiness endpoint and tune interval, timeout, and thresholds. A too-aggressive health check can mark healthy tasks as unhealthy; too lax and you may route traffic to failing tasks. When a target is marked unhealthy the ALB stops sending traffic to it, and ECS will replace the failed task based on the service desired count. Combine sensible health checks and autoscaling thresholds to create resilient, self-healing services that scale with demand. Service Auto-Scaling and Health Checks means use cpu or memory-based policies with sensible thresholds and tune alb health checks to prevent false positives and ensure stable scaling.. In practical terms, configure scaling policies and tune health checks for reliable applications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Common Deployment Failures & Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting ECS Fargate deployments often follows a predictable set of checks. If tasks fail to start or remain in PENDING, inspect CloudWatch logs and the task's stoppedReason. A common error is CannotPullContainerError: AccessDeniedException, which indicates the ecsTaskExecutionRole lacks permission to pull from ECR; check the execution role's policy and ensure it has ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchGetImage, and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer plus logs permissions. If the ALB returns 503 or targets remain unhealthy, verify security groups: the task SG must allow inbound traffic from the ALB SG on the container port, and the ALB SG must allow inbound 80 from client sources. Also confirm subnets have available IP addresses for awsvpc ENIs. If tasks crash due to resource limits, increase C P U or memory in the task definition. Finally, check health check paths and containerized application readiness. Use describe-tasks and describe-services, then review CloudWatch logs and the ALB target group health checks. Systematically checking IAM, security groups, subnets, and resource sizing will resolve most deployment failures. Common Deployment Failures & Fixes means check ecstaskexecutionrole permissions, security groups between alb and tasks, subnet ip availability, container logs, and task resource allocation.. In practical terms, diagnose failed starts, permission errors, and networking issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we shift from building container images to running them reliably at scale. You will learn what makes up Amazon ECS—clusters, task definitions, tasks, and services—and why choosing the right launch type matters. We'll focus on the Fargate launch type so you can run containers without provisioning EC2 instances. That means specifying C P U, memory, and networking while AWS handles the underlying servers. Practically, you'll see how to create a Fargate cluster, author a task definition that points to an image in ECR, and create a service that integrates with an Application Load Balancer. I will also explain how to enable service auto-scaling and the common misconfigurations that prevent tasks from running, such as missing permissions on the ecsTaskExecutionRole or incorrect security group rules. By the end of this lesson you'll understand the deployment flow and the safety checklist you should run before launching a production service. To ground this, we'll use an Nginx example pushed to ECR and deploy it to an ALB-backed, auto-scaled Fargate service so you can verify the DNS and clean up resources afterward. Ready to deploy your first Fargate service and reduce operational overhead?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify ECS's core components and explain their roles in running containers. You will learn to distinguish EC2 and Fargate launch types and select the best fit for a workload based on operational overhead and billing. You will deploy a containerized application to a Fargate cluster, registering a task definition, launching a service, and integrating an Application Load Balancer. Finally, you will configure basic service auto-scaling and apply troubleshooting steps for common failures such as image pull permission errors or misconfigured security groups. Each objective focuses on practical competence: naming components, writing a task definition, and validating networking and IAM. For example, when you write a task definition you will both choose C P U and memory values and attach the ecsTaskExecutionRole so the ECS agent can pull images and send logs. Practicing the CLI and console paths ensures you can repeat deployments and fix issues quickly. These skills let you operate containerized workloads securely and with predictable scaling behavior.

This second objectives slide emphasizes practical deployment skills. You'll create a Fargate cluster in the console or with the AWS CLI, register a task definition that uses the awsvpc network mode, and set appropriate C P U and memory values for your workload. You'll attach ecsTaskExecutionRole to let the ECS agent pull images from ECR and publish logs to CloudWatch. Then you'll create a service that runs a desired number of tasks and registers them with an Application Load Balancer's target group. You'll also enable service auto-scaling using C P U or custom CloudWatch metrics and practice scaling thresholds such as scale-out at 70 percent C P U and scale-in below 50 percent. Finally, you'll verify task health via ALB health checks and use the ALB DNS to confirm the application responds. These procedural skills let you deploy repeatable infrastructure both in the console and through automation with the AWS CLI, which helps teams deliver reliable container services consistently.

Let's define the four core ECS concepts and why each matters. A cluster is a logical collection where tasks and services run. Think of it as a name and grouping that can be backed by EC2 instances or Fargate; the choice affects who manages servers. A task definition is a declarative blueprint describing one or more containers, their images, C P U and memory, port mappings, networking mode, environment variables, and the execution IAM role. It is the unit you version and deploy. A task is an instantiation of that definition — one running set of containers. It lives inside a cluster and consumes the defined resources. A service ties the pieces together by specifying how many copies of the task should be running, performing health checks and restarting tasks when needed. Services also integrate with load balancers so traffic can be routed to healthy tasks. Common confusion comes from language: a task definition is not a running container, and a service is not a task; the service manages tasks created from a task definition. For example, when you update a task definition you must update the service to use the new revision so ECS will launch replacement tasks with the new configuration. Verify your ecsTaskExecutionRole and network settings before launching a service to avoid failures.

Choosing between EC2 and Fargate affects cost, control, and operational tasks. EC2 launch type gives you full control over worker nodes: you provision and patch EC2 instances, choose instance families, and can optimize cost with Reserved or Spot Instances for stable, predictable workloads. That control can yield cost savings for long-running services, but it requires you to manage capacity, OS updates, and scaling rules. Fargate abstracts away the nodes. You simply define C P U and memory for your tasks and AWS runs them. This serverless model minimizes operational overhead and charges you only for the C P U and memory your tasks use. It is ideal for variable or unpredictable workloads and for teams that want to focus on application logic. A common misconception is that Fargate is always more expensive; while Fargate can have higher per-unit costs, the operational savings and pay-per-use model often justify it for many workloads. Use EC2 when you need custom AMIs, specialized drivers, or deeper control over the host. Use Fargate for simplicity, faster onboarding, and consistent, serverless container execution. EC2 vs Fargate Launch Types means ec2 offers control and potential cost optimization for predictable workloads; fargate offers serverless simplicity and pay-for-use billing.. In practical terms, when to manage ec2 instances and when to use serverless fargate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk the deployment process step by step so you can repeat it reliably. Step one is creating a Fargate cluster; this reserves a logical environment name and readies ECS for tasks. Step two is authoring a task definition that specifies networkMode as awsvpc, an execution role, container image, port mapping, C P U, and memory. Step three registers that task definition and optionally uploads a JSON file via the CLI. Step four creates an Application Load Balancer and a target group configured for IP targets and an appropriate health check path. Step five creates the ECS service: choose Fargate, select the task definition, set the desired task count, and attach the target group so the ALB routes traffic to tasks. Finally, enable service auto-scaling with policies such as scale-out when C P U > 70 percent and scale-in when C P U < 50 percent. A common pitfall is forgetting to open port 80 in the ALB and task security groups, which blocks traffic even when tasks are running. Follow this process and verify each step with describe commands or the console status until the ALB returns the expected page.

Now we will examine a minimal task definition and explain the fields you must set for Fargate. The family names the task definition revision. Network mode must be awsvpc for Fargate to provide an elastic network interface per task. C P U and memory are specified as strings representing task-level resources. executionRoleArn should point to ecsTaskExecutionRole so the ECS agent can pull images from ECR and publish logs to CloudWatch. Under containerDefinitions you list each container with its image, port mappings, log configuration, and resource settings. Port mappings are needed for ALB routing. A frequent error is omitting the awslogs configuration so container logs do not arrive in CloudWatch, which makes troubleshooting harder. Another common issue is specifying too little C P U or memory; monitor CloudWatch to determine if tasks are throttled or crash. Use this JSON as a starting point, replace the ECR image URI with your repo, and register it using the AWS CLI register-task-definition command. This concrete example helps you avoid the most common omissions when authoring task definitions. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding how the Application Load Balancer connects to Fargate tasks is essential for validating deployments. In this architecture, an ALB listener receives HTTP traffic on port 80 and forwards it to a target group configured with target type ip. Each Fargate task receives an elastic network interface and an IP in your selected subnets, so the target group registers the task IPs as targets. Configure a health check path, for example root slash, that returns 200 OK so the ALB knows which targets are healthy. If a target fails health checks, the ALB removes it from routing and the ECS service will try to replace it to maintain the desired count. Security groups must permit inbound traffic from the ALB to the task on the container port, and the ALB's security group must permit inbound 80 from the internet or your client. Misconfigurations often involve security groups or health checks pointing to the wrong path. Always verify the ALB target group shows healthy targets before concluding the deployment is successful. Troubleshooting ECS Fargate deployments often follows a predictable set of checks. If tasks fail to start or remain in PENDING, inspect CloudWatch logs and the task's stoppedReason.
